questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Sound placed inside or outside the story
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish diegetic from non-diegetic sound
questions.stem: In the morning handover on the surgical ward, a nurse explains that the trolley rattle belongs to the room the characters stand in while the radio murmur reaches only the audience. What does that contrast make available?

options.text: It reverses the labels, treating the radio as diegetic and the trolley as non-diegetic sound
options.misconception: swaps diegetic and non-diegetic labels

options.text: It shows that both sounds are diegetic and that the nurse is being imprecise about the audience
options.misconception: insists every audible sound exists inside the story

options.text: It separates the sounds the characters can hear from the sound offered to the audience alone
It suggests neither sound is meaningful and the contrast is an artefact of the building
options.misconception: treats the contrast as incidental acoustics

questions.explanation: The trolley is heard by the characters, so it is diegetic; the radio reaches the audience alone, so it is not. The contrast lets the audience hear a commentary the characters cannot.
questions.hint: Ask who could hear each sound.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A reversal made of a scene
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of a reversal played without warning

stimulus.body: The night sister passes the play to the ward manager, noting that the last scene reverses everything the first scene promised. The actors have been told to play the reversal straight, as if nothing turned.

questions.stem: In the night handover on the children's ward, the sister reads the note about the reversal and asks what an audience takes from a reversal played straight rather than signalled.

options.text: The audience feels the reversal as ordinary, so the reversal lands without any effect at all
options.misconception: believes a straight delivery removes the reversal's force

options.text: The audience is asked to supply the irony themselves, which spreads the work of judgement outward
options.misconception: thinks ambiguity always equals audience collaboration

options.text: The reversal is intended as a puzzle to be solved before the final scene, not as an effect
options.misconception: reads the reversal as a puzzle with a solution

options.text: Because the staging marks nothing, the audience discovers the turn unawares and feels its shock

questions.explanation: Playing the reversal straight removes the signal that would let the audience prepare. The turn therefore arrives as an experience rather than a puzzle, and its force comes from the absence of warning.
questions.hint: Think about what the staging does not tell.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a soliloquy commits a character to
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a soliloquy binds its speaker to
questions.stem: On the night shift in the oncology day unit, a nurse observes that a character speaks alone on stage and is heard by nobody else. What is the character committed to by that speech?

options.text: The character is committed to the position they voice, since no one in the scene contradicts it
The character is committed to nothing, because a speech with no listener changes no facts
options.misconception: assumes unheard speech cannot commit anyone

options.text: The character is committed to sounding sincere, since an audience hears intention without reply
options.misconception: confuses being heard with sounding sincere

options.text: The character is committed to secrecy, since speaking aloud in company would expose the thought
options.misconception: reads soliloquy as deliberate concealment

questions.explanation: A soliloquy is a speech made where no one else can hear it, so no counter-voice corrects it. The audience is therefore shown a position the character is not yet performing for anyone else.
questions.hint: Ask who could answer the speech.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A pun doing argumentative work
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a pun can carry an argument
questions.stem: In the afternoon handover in the general medical ward, the nurse asks a colleague to explain how a pun in the play argues rather than merely decorates. Write the explanation she needs.

answer.exemplar: A pun does argumentative work when it makes one word carry two meanings at once, so that the second meaning attacks an idea the first meaning appears to support. It is not decoration added for wit; the joke is the mechanism by which the text makes its claim and puts pressure on a character who trusts the innocent sense.

questions.explanation: The task asks for an argument about a pun as a device. A strong answer names the double meaning, shows which sense carries the argument, and refuses to treat wit as decoration.
questions.hint: Name the two senses and the pressure.

questions.learningObjective: Describe the terms a prologue establishes
questions.stem: At the end of a shift in the cardiac ward, a nurse argues that the prologue fixes facts, tone and expectation before any character enters. Which description best explains that function?

options.text: The prologue withdraws the audience from the plot so that later scenes feel like episodes
options.misconception: treats the prologue as an escape from plot

options.text: The prologue settles what the audience will treat as given, so later claims are measured against it
The prologue introduces each character one by one, so nothing in the play depends on recognition
options.misconception: believes the prologue's job is character listing

options.text: The prologue foreshadows the ending so the audience watches the middle as inevitable
options.misconception: assumes the prologue simply spoils the ending

questions.explanation: A prologue establishes the terms the audience will accept as given, so later speeches argue against a fixed ground. Because the prologue supplies no counter-voice, its claims become the measure the play tests.
questions.hint: Think about the ground the play argues on.

options.text: Performance adds only the actors' faces, since the script already contains every sign that matters
options.misconception: reduces performance to visible acting alone

options.text: Performance adds nothing essential, so staging the text actually narrows what it means
options.misconception: believes staging can only narrow meaning

options.text: Performance adds tone through voices alone, because gesture and pace belong to the script
options.misconception: confines performance to vocal delivery

options.text: Performance adds timing, bodies and shared attention that the words only invite

questions.explanation: A printed script contains lines and stage directions, but not the duration of a pause or the pressure of a held look. Performance supplies those elements, so what it adds is interpretive rather than decorative.

questions.topic: Dialogue and monologue
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish dialogue from monologue by their conditions
questions.stem: Midway through the shift in the isolation bay, the nurse compares two scenes and asks what separates dialogue from monologue in the ways that matter.

options.text: Dialogue is quieter and monologue louder, so the difference is one of volume on the page
options.misconception: reduces the difference to volume alone

options.text: Dialogue is written in verse and monologue in prose, so the difference is one of form
options.misconception: believes verse versus prose marks the divide

options.text: Dialogue is exchanged and heard, while monologue is delivered and answers nobody
Dialogue is longer and monologue shorter, so the difference is one of length on the page
options.misconception: judges the forms by their length

questions.explanation: Dialogue depends on turn-taking, so each speech is shaped by a reply the character can hear. Monologue runs without a reply, which is why it commits the speaker more directly than the same words in dialogue.

questions.topic: Sound placed inside or outside the story
questions.learningObjective: Interpret sound laid under an occupied scene

stimulus.body: A student nurse mentions that the ward's own radio plays only when the characters are offstage. The sister says the audience hears it even during a scene the characters occupy, and she calls it a score rather than a source.

questions.stem: On the night handover in the isolation bay, the sister describes the radio that runs under a scene the characters occupy. What is the effect of that placement?

options.text: The radio becomes part of the room the characters inhabit, since the characters never comment on it
options.misconception: assumes unremarked sound is always diegetic

options.text: The radio works as an outside voice laid under the scene, colouring it for the audience alone
The radio proves the characters are deaf, because no one in the scene responds to it
options.misconception: reads silence about the sound as deafness

options.text: The radio is a mistake in the sound plan, since sound under a scene always confuses the house
options.misconception: treats the effect as a technical error

questions.explanation: Sound that continues under a scene the characters occupy functions as an external score rather than a source within the room. Because the characters never react to it, the audience alone hears it working on the scene.

questions.topic: A reversal made of a scene
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a repeated scene with a changed fact reveals
questions.stem: In the early handover in the maternity unit, the nurse describes a second scene that repeats the first with one crucial fact changed. What does that reversal accomplish?

options.text: It proves that the first scene carried no meaning, since the facts were never fixed to begin with
options.misconception: treats the reversal as voiding the first scene

options.text: It exposes what the first scene let the audience take for granted, making the earlier reading unstable
It doubles the plot so the audience must hold two complete and unrelated stories
options.misconception: believes repetition multiplies separate plots

options.text: It ends the action early so that the rest of the play can comment on what happened
options.misconception: reads the reversal as a way to end the action

questions.explanation: A reversal re-reads what the audience already accepted. Repeating a scene with one fact changed shows that earlier certainties were assumptions, so the audience must revise its judgement.
questions.hint: Ask what the first scene let you assume.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a soliloquy commits a character to
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a soliloquy commits without concealing
questions.stem: During the handover in the cardiac ward, the nurse is asked what a soliloquy commits a character to and why that commitment is not simply privacy. Write the answer she needs.

answer.exemplar: A soliloquy commits the character to the position voiced, because nothing in the scene can correct it: no other character hears, objects or qualifies. It is not private speech in the sense of being hidden, since the audience hears every word. The exposure rather than the secrecy is what makes the commitment real.

questions.explanation: The answer must connect the lack of a listener to the force of the commitment and resist treating the speech as merely private. The exemplar links correction and exposure.
questions.hint: Focus on who cannot answer the speech.

options.text: Puns are rare in serious plays, so their rarity shows playwrights avoid them for argument
options.misconception: argues from rarity instead of function

options.text: Puns shorten a scene's length, which shows they are practical rather than argumentative
options.misconception: confuses brevity with argumentative purpose

options.text: Puns distract the audience from the plot, so audiences remember them and forget the argument
options.misconception: treats memorability as proof of distraction

options.text: A pun makes one word carry an argument, so the joke is the mechanism rather than a break

questions.explanation: The rebuttal has to locate the pun inside the argument rather than beside it. A double meaning lets a single word press on an idea a character holds, which is a claim-making function rather than a comic interval.
questions.hint: Ask what the joke makes the words do.

The prologue has no effect on the play because the characters disregard everything it announces

questions.learningObjective: Infer what different stagings of one text reveal
questions.stem: After a night on the neurology ward, the nurse notes that the same page of script produces different plays with two different directors. What does that fact suggest about performance?

options.text: The script leaves choices open that performance must make, so staging interprets as it realises
The script is incomplete, so no performance can be faithful to what the author intended
options.misconception: calls the script faulty rather than open

options.text: The directors contradict each other, and only one can be reading the text correctly
options.misconception: assumes there is a single correct staging

options.text: The script is deliberately ambiguous, so the text refuses to support any clear meaning

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Dialogue and monologue
questions.learningObjective: Explain why brief replies can commit a character more

stimulus.body: Two students on the maternity ward argue about a scene where one character talks at length while the other only says yes. The charge nurse rules that the quiet character is the more committed of the two.

questions.stem: In the maternity unit handover, the charge nurse's ruling about the quiet character and the talkative one is best explained how?

options.text: The brief replies leave the character exposed, since each yes carries a commitment nobody answers
The long speech is the commitment, because sheer length of talk shows how far a character has gone
options.misconception: measures commitment by how much is said

options.text: The talkative character is more committed, since the audience hears more of that character's reasoning
options.misconception: confuses speech length with the depth of feeling

options.text: Neither character is committed, since the pair are speaking only out of politeness to each other
options.misconception: dismisses the scene as empty convention

questions.explanation: A character who only answers yes cannot qualify the position they accept, so each short reply amounts to a concession. Commitment turns on what a character is bound to, not on how much they speak.
questions.hint: Consider what the short replies cannot withdraw.

questions.stem: During the shift handover in the psychiatric unit, the nurse explains that the buzzer heard at the start belongs to the story and the applause does not. Which statement captures the difference?

The buzzer and applause both exist in the story world, but at different volumes for the audience

options.misconception: reverses which sound the characters hear

options.misconception: treats both sounds as meaningless effects

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A reversal made of a scene
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a reversal made of a scene works on an audience
questions.stem: At the afternoon handover in the oncology unit, the nurse asks how a reversal made of a scene works, and what the audience must do with it. Write the explanation she needs.

answer.exemplar: A reversal made of a scene repeats the earlier action under one changed fact, so that the audience discovers the earlier scene was resting on an assumption rather than a certainty. Its work is diagnostic: the repeat exposes the terms the first scene had quietly taken for granted, and the audience must revise its earlier reading rather than merely watch a new event.

questions.explanation: The answer should define the reversal as a repeated scene with a changed fact and explain its diagnostic effect on the audience's earlier reading. The exemplar does both.

options.text: The objection fails because soliloquies are rare enough that audiences barely notice them
options.misconception: dismisses the claim by counting how rare the form is

options.text: The objection holds, since hearing a position voiced does not prove the character believes it
The objection fails because the character cannot hear the audience and so cannot perform for it
options.misconception: thinks an unheard speech cannot be performance

options.text: The objection holds only if the character never speaks to anyone else in the play
options.misconception: restricts the doubt to plays without other speeches

questions.explanation: A soliloquy gives the audience a position without any mark of reliability, so voicing and endorsing come apart. The fair objection accepts that gap instead of assuming every voiced belief is a settled belief.
questions.hint: Voicing is not the same as holding.

options.misconception: treats the pun as ending the scene's tone

questions.explanation: When a pun turns a character's phrasing back on himself, the argument continues through the joke. The character cannot deflect it, so the comic device is also the pressure that keeps the claim alive.

questions.topic: What a prologue fixes before the play
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a prologue cannot settle
questions.stem: During the early handover in the renal unit, the nurse considers what a prologue fixes and asks which of these it cannot do.

options.text: It cannot introduce the setting, because the first scene always has to establish the place
options.misconception: thinks the first scene must establish the setting

options.text: It cannot fix the play's argument, since an argument only exists once characters disagree
It cannot signal the tone, because tone is carried entirely by the actors' delivery
options.misconception: believes tone lives only in performance

options.text: It cannot supply facts the audience needs, because those facts arrive through dialogue
options.misconception: claims facts must come through dialogue

questions.learningObjective: Identify what a performed pause adds to a printed line

questions.stem: Between shifts in the renal unit, the ward manager describes the taped pause before the angry speech. What does the pause contribute that the page cannot?

options.text: The pause confirms the script's intention, because the actor merely follows what was written
options.misconception: treats performance as obedience to the page

options.text: The pause supplies no meaning, since timing belongs to the director and not to the actor
options.misconception: excludes actors from interpretive choices

The pause shows that the audience's silence is a technical fault in the recording
options.misconception: blames the recording rather than the performance

questions.explanation: The page fixes the words and their order but not how long a silence lasts before them. A held pause lets the audience read the anger as controlled rather than merely stated, so the timing carries argument.
questions.hint: Read the anger as something restrained.

questions.learningObjective: Compare the commitments made in dialogue and monologue

options.misconception: ties authority to the length of a speech

options.text: The exchange commits both speakers to equal certainty, since a reply always matches the point

The long speech commits nobody, since a speaker alone is only rehearsing an argument

questions.topic: Sound placed inside or outside the story
questions.learningObjective: Explain the difference in force between in-world and external sound
questions.stem: In the handover on the stroke unit, the nurse needs a written explanation of why sound inside the story differs in force from sound outside it. Write the answer she can hand over.

answer.exemplar: Sound inside the story world is subject to the world's own rules, so a clock, a bell or a footstep carries the time, the weather and the location of whoever hears it. Sound outside the story has no character who could hear it and therefore no place or hour, which is exactly why it can comment on a scene it does not belong to.

questions.explanation: The written answer must contrast what in-world sound can carry with what external sound cannot, and ground the difference in who could hear each. The exemplar does this.
questions.hint: Compare what each sound can know.

questions.topic: What a prologue fixes before the play
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the tone of a prologue and what it licenses

stimulus.body: A note from the drama group says the prologue should sound like a legal notice read aloud to the audience by someone who believes it. The group argued that a tone of certainty there changes what the play is arguing about.

The commitment is therefore real but unsupported: the character has bound themselves in public to something the play has not yet tested.

questions.explanation: The answer must state the commitment and the reason it holds, and avoid treating the speech as private. The exemplar ties the absence of a listener to an unsupported public claim.
questions.hint: Say why no one can qualify it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A pun doing argumentative work
questions.learningObjective: Defend the claim that a pun makes a character their own critic
questions.stem: Throughout the handover in the respiratory unit, the nurse argues that a pun can make a character their own worst critic. Which argument fits?

options.text: Because a pun hides the speaker's meaning, so the audience cannot say what the character meant
options.misconception: treats the pun as obscuring the meaning

options.text: Because the audience enjoys the joke more than they follow the argument
options.misconception: grounds the claim in audience enjoyment

options.text: Because a pun gives the character a rest from the argument, so the scene can move on
options.misconception: reads the pun as an interruption

options.text: Because the second sense of the pun returns the speaker's own claim to them for judgement

questions.explanation: The argument works because the pun turns the speaker's vocabulary against the position it was used to support. The character becomes the object of the judgement they were directing at others.
questions.hint: Ask whose claim comes back.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a prologue fixes before the play
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a prologue cannot fix
questions.stem: Between medication rounds in the neonatal unit, the nurse lists what a prologue fixes and which of these it does not fix.

options.text: It does not fix the plot, because a plot only exists once characters begin to act
options.misconception: claims the prologue shapes the plot

options.text: It does not fix the outcome, because the outcome is what the play's later argument decides
It does not fix the tone, because tone is carried by the actors' choices at rehearsal
options.misconception: claims the prologue sets the tone firmly

options.text: It does not fix the facts, because facts belong to the scenes in which they are tested
options.misconception: claims the prologue supplies testable facts

questions.explanation: The item that a prologue cannot fix is the one the play exists to decide. Fixing the outcome would end the argument in advance, so the prologue settles terms and tone while leaving the result open.
questions.hint: Ask what the play exists to decide.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Play text and what performance adds
questions.learningObjective: Identify a genuine contribution performance makes
questions.stem: At the evening handover in the geriatrics unit, the nurse asks which of these is a contribution performance makes to a play text.

options.text: It supplies the missing motive for a character whose actions the script leaves unexplained
options.misconception: credits performance with adding motive

options.text: It fixes the rhythm of the play, since the page cannot say how fast a line should land
It supplies the theme, since the theme is only visible once the actors have spoken
options.misconception: makes performance the source of the theme

options.text: It supplies the historical setting, which the script assumes but never states
options.misconception: treats performance as adding setting

questions.explanation: The page can state a motive, a theme or a setting if the playwright wants them stated. What it cannot state is rhythm, so the speed at which a line lands is decided in performance.
questions.hint: Ask what the page cannot specify.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Dialogue and monologue
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a silent listener can be the character who changes

stimulus.body: A student records that in one scene two characters argue in turn, and in the next a single character talks for the whole scene while the other listens in silence. The note says the silent listener is the one who changes.

questions.stem: In the geriatrics unit handover, the student's claim about the silent listener being the one who changes is best explained how?

options.text: Silence has no content, so the listener cannot be said to have changed at all
options.misconception: treats silence as empty of meaning

options.text: The listener changes because speeches are easier to resist than silences
options.misconception: grounds the change in the ease of resistance

options.text: The silent listener must answer the speech to herself, since nobody else will do it for her
The listener changes because the actors improvise differently in the silent scene
options.misconception: attributes the change to improvisation

questions.explanation: Public replies each answer the other, but in the monologue scene nobody answers, so the listening character carries the response herself. That is where the change happens.
questions.hint: Ask who answers inside the silence.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Sound placed inside or outside the story
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one sound can belong to the story and another to the performance
questions.stem: Early in the handover on the stroke rehabilitation bay, the nurse asks why a sound can belong to the story while another belongs to the performance.

options.text: Because one is available to the characters as part of their world and the other is not
Because one is written into the script and the other is left to the sound engineer
options.misconception: splits the two by who writes them

options.text: Because one is loud enough to be heard and the other is quiet enough to be missed
options.misconception: judges the sounds by volume alone

options.text: Because one happens on stage and the other happens in the wings or the stalls
options.misconception: locates the difference in stage geography

questions.explanation: The distinction is about availability, not loudness or authorship. A sound the characters could react to belongs to their world; one no character can receive belongs to the performance and may comment on the scene.
questions.hint: Ask who could react to it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A reversal made of a scene
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a reversal made of a scene works on an audience
questions.stem: At the start of the handover in the renal unit, the nurse writes out how a reversal made of a scene works on an audience. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: A reversal made of a scene works by repetition with a difference. The audience watches a scene it thinks it has understood, and then watches it again with one fact altered. Because the staging can stay identical, the change cannot be blamed on atmosphere or accident, so the audience must decide what the earlier scene really meant and revise the reading it had already made.

questions.explanation: The explanation must describe the repeat, the changed fact and the audience's need to revise its reading. The exemplar covers all three in order.
questions.hint: Say what the audience must revise.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a soliloquy commits a character to
questions.learningObjective: Dispute the claim that a soliloquy is the most honest speech
questions.stem: On the late shift in the respiratory unit, the nurse disputes the claim that a soliloquy is the most honest speech in a play. Which argument is strongest?

options.text: A soliloquy is written for an audience, so its candour is a performance rather than a proof
Soliloquies are usually short, so the form has no room for the careful evasion it promises
options.misconception: attacks the form using its typical length

options.text: Soliloquies are spoken aloud, and anyone speaking aloud is performing for someone
options.misconception: reasons from the mere fact of speaking aloud

options.text: Soliloquies usually occur in private, so they are bound to be more truthful than speeches
options.misconception: assumes privacy guarantees truth

questions.explanation: The strongest objection notes that a soliloquy is still delivered to an audience, so its apparent frankness is a chosen mode of address. What looks like unfiltered truth is therefore a performance like any other.
questions.hint: Ask who the soliloquist is still speaking to.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A pun doing argumentative work
questions.learningObjective: Select the pun that would carry an argument in a play about debt
questions.stem: In the final handover of the night shift in the maternity unit, the nurse asks which pun would do argumentative work in a play about debt.

options.text: A pun on a word for the lender, so the audience laughs at the character's creditor
options.misconception: makes the joke's target the creditor

options.text: A pun on a word for money, so the theme of debt is stated in a memorable way
options.misconception: treats memorability as the pun's function

options.text: A pun on a word the debtor uses, so his own phrase exposes the terms he has accepted
A pun on a word for the market, so the play ends on a note of economic commentary
options.misconception: moves the pun's target outside the characters

questions.explanation: The pun does argumentative work when the double sense falls inside the character's own language. A word the debtor uses, turned to show the terms he has accepted, makes him the object of the argument.
questions.hint: Find the word the character himself supplies.
